claims.text: Nominally equiatomic Nb-Ta-Ti-V is a refractory high-entropy alloy that can exist as a single-phase solid solution.
Accurate prediction of Tm, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for refractory HEAs requires a hybrid DFT-CALPHAD methodology.
DFT calculations of lattice stability and phonon density of states can supply the solid-phase thermodynamics needed by the hybrid method.
Standard approaches commonly rely on ideal-solution models or binary interaction parameters.
Ideal-solution models and binary interaction parameters fail to capture severe lattice distortion and complex chemical disorder in HEAs.
Failure to capture lattice distortion and chemical disorder leads to inaccurate descriptions of the liquid phase.
Special quasirandom structures can represent the random distribution of elements in the disordered solid.
DFT-SQS calculations can determine cohesive and vibrational free-energy contributions for the disordered solid.
A lattice-distortion correction to the liquid entropy can correct ideal-solution assumptions in CALPHAD.
The melting temperature occurs where the Gibbs free energies of the solid and liquid phases are equal.
Configurational entropy enhances the thermodynamic stability of the HEA solid phase.
The sluggish-diffusion effect associated with lattice distortion lowers the vibrational entropy of the solid.
Standard CALPHAD models often underestimate solid stability or overestimate liquid entropy in HEAs.
Combining DFT-SQS solid thermodynamics with a non-ideal liquid model incorporating mixing entropy and short-range order will improve melting-temperature prediction.
The entropy of fusion can be obtained from the difference in vibrational and configurational entropy between the disordered solid and liquid.
Refractory HEAs are expected to have entropy of fusion above 10.5 J/mol·K because of residual disorder in the liquid.
The hybrid method will predict melting temperatures within ±50 K of available experimental values.
The predicted entropy of fusion will be 10–20% above Richard's-rule values, typically 12–14 J/mol·K.
DFT-derived phonon contributions will produce heat-capacity trends that agree with experiment better than empirical models.
The method is valid primarily for single-phase, high-mixing-entropy solid solutions and may fail for systems forming intermetallic compounds or undergoing phase separation near melting.
